q-107802.name: Question 1
q-107802.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1-3x-3y}{x+y}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
q-107802.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1-3(x+y)}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{1-3z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1-2z}{z}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{1-2z}{z}.$

q-107802.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=1−3x−3yx+y. Using a substitution of the form z=x+y, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

a
1+zz
b
1−2zz
c
1−3z2z
d
1+3z
e
1+z2z
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get dydx=1−3(x+y)x+y.

Then, we make the substitution z=x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−1. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−1=1−3zz

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=1−2zz. Therefore, f(z)=1−2zz.

q-108736.name: Question 2
q-108736.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}+6xy+3{y}^{2}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
q-108736.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3(x+y)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =3{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3{z}^{2}+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=3{z}^{2}+1.$

Consider the differential equation dydx=3x2+6xy+3y2. Using a substitution of the form z=x+y, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

a
3z2−2
b
6z2−1
c
3z2
d
6z2+2
e
3z2+1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get dydx=3(x+y)2.

Then, we make the substitution z=x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−1. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−1=3z2

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z), we get dzdx=3z2+1. Therefore, f(z)=3z2+1.

q-108742.name: Question 3
q-108742.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=20y-12x.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=5y-3x,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
q-108742.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4(5y-3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=5y-3x.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=5\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3).
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3) & =4z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=20z-3.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=20z-3.$

a
1−10z

4z

20z

20z−3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get dydx=4(5y−3x).

q-108857.name: Question 4
q-108857.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{9x-3y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=y+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
q-108857.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3(3x-y)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=3x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{9z-2}{3z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3z}{9z-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{3z}{9z-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\int (1+\frac{2}{9z-2})\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}(z+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9z-2|) & =x+K \\ z+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9z-2| & =3x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-y+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|27x-9y-2| & =3x+C \\ \frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|27x-9y-2| & =y+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=27x-9y-2.
$$

Consider the differential equation dydx=29x−3y.

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form 29ln⁡|g(x,y)|=y+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
27x−9y−2
b
3x−y
c
27x−9y+3
d
3x−y+1
e
6x−2y−3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation. dydx=23(3x−y)

Then, we make the substitution z=3x−y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=3−dydx⟹dydx=3−dzdx. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 3−dzdx=23z

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=9z−23z.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

3z9z−2dzdx=1∫3z9z−2dz=∫dx13∫(1+29z−2)dz=∫dx13(z+29ln⁡|9z−2|)=x+Kz+29ln⁡|9z−2|=3x+C where C=3K.

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: 3x−y+29ln⁡|27x−9y−2|=3x+C29ln⁡|27x−9y−2|=y+C

Therefore, g(x,y)=27x−9y−2.

q-149753.name: Question 5
q-149753.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2-\sqrt{9x+9y}}{3\sqrt{x+y}}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
q-149753.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2-3\sqrt{x+y}}{3\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{2-3\sqrt{z}}{3\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3\sqrt{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{3}{2}\int \sqrt{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ {z}^{3/2} & =x+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
(x+y)^{3/2}=x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=(x+y)^{3/2}.
$$
